# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: Evolution, Challenges, and Future Horizons

## Introduction
Metallic drug-eluting stents (DES) represent the current gold standard for percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), offering excellent acute luminal gain and low rates of restenosis. However, permanent metallic implants impose a lifelong physical limitation on the coronary vessel, preventing normal vasomotion, precluding surgical bypass graft anastomosis to the stented segment, and predisposing patients to very late adverse events such as neoatherosclerosis. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to provide temporary mechanical support and drug delivery to prevent early recoil and restenosis, subsequently undergoing complete resorption to restore the native vessel’s physiology—a concept termed "vascular restorative therapy" [1-4]. Early-generation devices sought to establish this paradigm by utilizing biocompatible polymers, primarily poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), which degrade over time into water and carbon dioxide [5].

## First-Generation Polymeric Scaffolds and Pivotal Trials
The Absorb everolimus-eluting BVS (Abbott Vascular) was the pioneering device in this field. Initial first-in-human studies, including the ABSORB Cohort A and Cohort B trials, demonstrated the feasibility of BVS implantation with progressive scaffold degradation, restoration of vasomotion, and late luminal gain at long-term follow-up [1-3]. These promising early results led to several large-scale, randomized clinical trials comparing the Absorb BVS to the standard-of-care metallic everolimus-eluting stent (EES) [6,7].

While intermediate-term trials showed comparable safety and efficacy, longer-term outcomes revealed a disturbing signal. The ABSORB II, ABSORB III, and ABSORB IV trials, as well as the independent AIDA trial, demonstrated a significant increase in target lesion failure (TLF) and, most critically, scaffold thrombosis (ST) with BVS compared to metallic EES [6-12]. These safety concerns were particularly pronounced in the very late phase (>1 year post-implantation), where very late scaffold thrombosis (VLST) occurred at rates significantly higher than those observed with metallic DES [11,12]. This excess risk was also highlighted in complex clinical scenarios, such as ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) [13,14]. Consequently, the first-generation Absorb BVS was withdrawn from commercial use, prompting deep clinical introspection.

## Mechanisms of Scaffold Thrombosis and the PSP Protocol
To address the high rates of ST, researchers investigated the underlying mechanical and biological mechanisms of scaffold failure. Large multicenter registries and systemic reviews established that the relatively thick struts of the first-generation Absorb BVS (150 $\mu$m, compared to approximately 80 $\mu$m for contemporary metallic DES) created significant rheological disturbances, flow separation, and platelet activation [15,16]. Furthermore, intravascular imaging modalities, such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS), revealed that late scaffold discontinuity, malapposition, underexpansion, and incomplete resorption of polymeric remnants were key triggers for VLST [17,18].

These mechanistic insights highlighted that BVS could not be implanted like conventional metallic stents [19]. This led to the development of the "PSP" protocol to optimize implantation technique: meticulous lesion **P**re-dilatation, precise **S**izing of the scaffold (avoiding mismatch), and systematic **P**ost-dilatation using non-compliant balloons at high pressure [20,21]. Clinical registries demonstrated that adherence to the PSP protocol significantly reduced the risk of both early and late scaffold thrombosis, underscoring that optimal implantation technique is as critical as device design [21,22].

## Next-Generation Scaffolds: Magnesium and Thin-Strut Technology
The setbacks of first-generation PLLA scaffolds spurred the development of novel materials and designs. Bioresorbable metallic alloys, particularly magnesium-based scaffolds, represent a major evolutionary step. Early work on non-drug-eluting magnesium stents by Erbel et al. [23] demonstrated the feasibility of metallic resorption. This paved the way for drug-eluting versions, such as the DREAMS-1 scaffold evaluated in the BIOSOLVE-I trial [24]. Subsequently, the sirolimus-eluting Magmaris scaffold (DREAMS-2) was developed, showing rapid resorption within 12 months and favorable outcomes in the BIOSOLVE-II [25] and BIOSOLVE-IV registries [26], with low target lesion failure rates and no definite scaffold thrombosis.

Simultaneously, polymeric BVS underwent structural refinement. To overcome the limitations of 150 $\mu$m struts, next-generation polymeric scaffolds have focused on reducing strut thickness to less than 100 $\mu$m. The Fantom scaffold, a thin-strut, radiopaque, tyrosine-polycarbonate-based BVS, demonstrated promising safety and efficacy in its first-in-human trial [27]. Similarly, the Firesorb sirolimus-eluting BVS, featuring thin PLLA struts (~86 $\mu$m), showed favorable 1-year clinical and angiographic performance with minimal late lumen loss and no thrombosis [28].

## Conclusion and Future Directions
The clinical journey of BVS has been a paradigm of rapid technological adoption followed by safety-driven correction and refinement [29,30]. While first-generation thick-strut polymeric scaffolds suffered from elevated thrombosis rates, they taught the interventional cardiology community vital lessons regarding the necessity of precise implantation techniques and the limitations of polymer physics. Today, next-generation thin-strut polymeric and magnesium-based BVS offer superior deliverability, faster resorption, and optimized vascular healing [29]. If ongoing randomized trials can validate their long-term safety and efficacy against state-of-the-art metallic DES, BVS may yet fulfill their promise of vascular restoration and redefine the future of percutaneous coronary revascularization.
